articles.title: Renaissance of Magic in Athens - 1924
articles.author: Κ. Φαλτάιτς
articles.excerpt: The case of the Beautiful Church and the injury of stockbroker Hatzipanagiotis spark Athenians' interest in spiritualism, hypnotism and occult sciences.

image.alt: Renaissance of magic in Athens (1924)

content.value: Renaissance of Magic in Athens – 1924
The vision of the 'Beautiful Church' continues to hold Athenians in a state of excitement, which we can say is advancing day by day on an upward scale.

The stockbroker Hatzipanagiotis, who was found with five serious bullet wounds beneath a pine tree at the Beautiful Church, has not yet managed to gather his memory and tell the forensic doctors, the investigating authorities and journalists how and where he was wounded.

The gap that exists at this point in his memory and the involvement, at the margins or at the center of the whole affair, of various persons who have a connection to the practice of so-called occult sciences — whether hypnotism, magic, or divination — gave occasion both to the Investigation and to investigative journalism to consider whether behind the crime of the Beautiful Church one should seek not only the woman, but also spiritualism, hypnotism, divination, astrology and in general the entire mysterious medley of occult science.
The drama played out around the wounding of stockbroker Hatzipanagiotis coincided with the most topical period for Athenians.
Never before had Athenians been so interested in psychic phenomena and their investigation as they are today.
From Tahrán Bey, the fakir who appeared in Athens a year ago, to the pseudo-fakirs and pseudo-hypnotists who followed, Athenians have advanced greatly in psychic matters.
Today almost everyone is involved with spiritualism, hypnotism, dream interpretation, palmistry, suggestion and influence, and the branches of occult science.
Compared to Europe and America, where thousands of spiritualist organizations operate and hundreds of magazines are published, Athenians are still considered behind.
The Painter Apostolidis
In the Hatzipanagiotis drama two figures appear to hold the threads of the mystery: a coffee-cup reader who predicted the attack, and the painter I. Apostolidis, who is said to have hypnotized him.
Apostolidis, known for his character and artistic talent, does not appear to be connected to those responsible for the drama.
Every summer he travels to Skiathos to capture the landscapes that Papadiamantis rendered through writing.
His return to Athens is expected to shed light on aspects of the drama, especially those concerning the character of Hatzipanagiotis and the hypnotic experiments.
Spiritualism in Athens
Athens appears to be in a period of renaissance of magic, as are other European and American metropolises.
Several Societies for Psychical Research have recently been founded, the most well-known being those under Mr. Tanagras and the 'Dawn'.
At the same time the number of doctors applying hypnotism and suggestion as therapeutic means is increasing, as is their use by the police.
Magic is becoming a profession, often more lucrative than the rest.
It remains paradoxical that works of well-known spiritualist scientists have not yet been translated into Greek.
However, with the spiritualist frenzy of the era, the publication of an entire spiritualist library is expected.
Author: K. Falteits

articles.title: A Thousand Sorcerers in Athens and Piraeus 1933 - Barmpanastasis and His Devils
articles.author: Ε. ΘΩΜΟΠΟΥΛΟΣ
articles.excerpt: Athens was 'flooded with sorcerers'. A report on charlatans who exploit the naive, the distinction from scientific mediums, and the case of Barmpanastasis.

image.alt: A thousand sorcerers in Athens and Piraeus - Barmpanastasis and his devils (1933)

content.value: A Thousand Sorcerers in Athens and Piraeus 1933 – Barmpanastasis and His Devils
SCIENTIFIC MEDIUMS AND THE SORCERERS WHO FLEECE THE HANDBAGS OF NAIVE WOMEN. — BARMPANASTASIS WITH THE FAKIR SHEIKH’S MANUSCRIPT. — THE RECIPES THAT BRING HAPPINESS.

Athens has been flooded with… sorcerers! The Police, and in particular the Morality Department, have for some time been unable to keep up with the chase after these strange characters who, amid a phantasmagorical staging of red cloths and skulls, promise the credulous — and above all their endless female clientele — the return to the arms of unfaithful lovers, marriage to wealthy bridegrooms, and, in a word, paradise on earth.

The phenomenon is not entirely new to the Greeks. It begins in the era of the Oracle at Delphi, and the historiography of this profession tells us that one of its most notable victims was, in the last century, Queen Amalia! In order to have children and not lose her throne, the unfortunate queen spent everything she had on sorcerers and witches.
THEY EVEN HAVE ASSOCIATIONS

Lately, however, this exotic profession has seen an astonishing growth. There is scarcely a district of Athens or Piraeus that does not have its own “den”, where gods and demons are summoned and commanded with unintelligible words and with the performance of strange recipes — as was done by Mavridis, arrested the day before yesterday, whose exploits the “Akropolis” dealt with yesterday — in order to grant the longed-for happiness to the sorcerers’ clients, male and female. This astonishing growth, which is not checked despite the severe penalties of the courts, has two principal causes.

The first and chief one is popular misery combined with immorality. Poor girls who have given themselves to merciless lovers imagine that, with the help of the sorcerers, they will legitimise their relations.

Others again believe that they will secure a lucrative profession. Countless too are those who pay, and pay well, the sorcerers and witches, with the notion that they will learn from their lips the first number of the lottery.

The second and perhaps more important cause is the spread of the theories of the Society for Psychical Research. Its scientific work, directed with such noble passion by Mr Tanagras, has been misunderstood by the naive. The Society for Psychical Research has, as is well known, trained and established numerous mediums (scientifically intuitive women, as Mr Tanagras calls them), who work and receive clients under the protection of the Police. Their work, however, is purely scientific (hypnotism, telepathy and clairvoyance), as we shall analyse in the course of our investigation, and has no connection whatever with the sorcerers whom the criminal law pursues. They do not foretell the future, nor do they promise to rekindle the amorous ardour of the unfaithful, nor do they hand out imaginary mansions, nor do they announce lucky lottery numbers in advance.

Indeed, in order to combat those who prey upon the wallets and handbags of the naive, they have formed an association, whose board consists of the ladies and young ladies Nikolaidou, Zakynthinou, Karyati, Kassandras and Pavlatou, with honorary president Mrs Alexandra Choremi, one of the most fervent adherents of the theories concerning psychical and spiritualist phenomena.
But the unofficial sorcerers too have formed an association and confer among themselves, in order to advance their interests and to forestall pursuit by the Police.

This, at least, is what the excellent sergeant of the Morality Department, Mr N. Panagiotopoulos, has established from his special investigations. He assures us that about a thousand sorcerers and witches keep magnificent “dens” in Athens and skim the wallets of the naive. Armies of silly geese — as Mr Tanagras calls the female clientele of these rogues — offer up everything they have and have not, to indulge every kind of weakness and folly.
Out of this numerous fraternity of Athenian sorcerers, their fearful works and the tragicomic sufferings of their victims, we shall give what is of the most sensational interest.
As the ace of aces, then, in this diabolical profession, the Police have characterised Anastasios Vlysidis, called by his clientele Uncle Anastasis.
He has acquired from his profession a three-storey mansion on Ferron Street, and characteristic of his fame is his clientele, three-quarters of which comes from the upper social class.

Barely a month ago the Police closed the… gates of that most luxuriously furnished den, following an anonymous letter. They could not have suspected that inside the luxurious mansion there was a man who summoned assemblies of devils to satisfy the appetites of an endless female clientele.
Magnificent in appearance himself, always in impeccable dress and with his own motor car, he comes from Pontus.

His brazenness was such that he did not hesitate to declare, both to the Police and to the Magistrates’ Court that convicted him, that a fakir had entrusted him with a manuscript on whose pages all the recipes were written.
With these, he added, all the spirits arrive at once and obey his wishes immediately.
He was asked to produce the manuscript. He answered with the same brazenness that he had chewed the manuscript and that it was in his stomach.
— Why? asked the police officer Mr Pantelis.
— Because that was the order of my arch-sorcerer father. I swallowed it as soon as I had learned properly what was written inside it, but I have not digested it. It remains intact inside my stomach.
— My assistants, he said, are together with the manuscript in my belly. Pay attention here and keep quiet.

At his prompting the door of the police office was also closed, so that no one should interrupt the general attention. The most likely explanation is that he wanted to work suggestion on all the police officers — and he succeeded.

The enormous belly of the bulky Barmpanastasis began to swell dangerously. It reached as far as his chest. It swayed to right and to left. The police officers had been so far worked upon that they told him to stop. They believed he was about to burst in front of them like a balloon.
He was bellowing like a buffalo besides, and then said:
— See, I have them inside me and I do with them whatever I want. Watch!
He then began to waggle his finger, and an inkwell that stood on the table in the other corner fell to the floor, without anyone having touched it.
The scientific explanation of the phenomenon is that the exceedingly crafty old fellow is a subject possessing psychokinesis. /
Not even his psychokinesis did he admit to in court, and for that reason it convicted him. Which is curious, given how many victims he had and the wealth he amassed from the faith they placed in him.
The room in which he worked, in the luxurious mansion on Ferron Street, was full of black cloths. Black too were the furnishings, and on the floor the hide of an all-black bear.
He alone was in white, seated on a very low round stool. He wore a white turban, a white caftan, and on his chest, embroidered, a bony hand.
“Mademoiselles” and ladies who came in one by one to ask for and receive his counsel were seized with a shudder.
The contrast of the black décor with the white exotic costume was enough to fill the souls of the naive clients with awe.
The home-grown fakir spoke abruptly:
— Quickly! What do you want?
His voice was deep and cavernous, as much as the roguery of the business required.
On his right palm a skull and two bones were roughly drawn.
He would open his palm as the woman client sat opposite him trembling, and after a few minutes he would tell her her full name.
This made the naive victim feel, along with the awe, still greater confidence in this superhuman Uncle Anastasis.

And the phenomenon, as Mr Tanagras explains to us, is of the simplest: it is a matter of the power of self-concentration and of telepathy, which many people possess, without being able, however, to change the fortune or the will of others, as the charlatans of sorcery promise.

In any case, the victims, after recounting to the “devil-man” — the name and the thing alike — what they were asking for, and paying the price of the service, received their recipe, written out on little red slips of paper.
But it was not only that they received them and had to carry them out at the first hour of every night, on the first day of the week and on the first day of the month.
They had, after memorising the contents, to chew them and swallow them, without any other human eye seeing them; otherwise they lost their magical power and the desired result was not achieved.
The purpose of this “extreme” order of the sorcerer’s was obvious: he took care that no evidence should exist.
But by this wish of his he had caused all his victims to resort later to the pharmacists for laxatives.

articles.excerpt: The skeleton of an elderly person is found near the Piraeus ISAP station, with witnesses speaking of witches, sorcery and possible crime.

image.alt: Discovery of a skeleton near the Piraeus ISAP station in 1925

content.value: Mystery surrounds the skeleton found near the Piraeus ISAP station. It has not yet been established who was the elderly woman who abandoned the skeleton among the refuse.
The police sub-inspector of the 3rd Precinct, Mr. P. Barmpetseas, who is conducting the relevant investigation, has formed the opinion that the matter involves sorcery.

Maria Georgios Marketou, a neighbourhood resident, was questioned and testified that witches in Piraeus use human skeletons either by burning the bones into powder or exposing them to rain for the extraction of omens.

The elderly woman, who appears to have been one of them, left the skeleton uncovered so it would get wet. The number of such witches, according to testimonies, increased after the arrival of refugees from Asia Minor, most of whom reside in Kokkinia.
Witness Vas. Giakoumakis testified that a neighbourhood child saw the elderly woman, dressed in black, emptying the bones and lighting a fire at the spot — an act considered a sign of sorcery.
Despite the indications of magic, the possibility of a crime cannot be excluded. Perhaps the skeleton belonged to a victim that the elderly woman was keeping and abandoned out of fear of exposure.
The skeleton was almost complete, with the bones detached and bearing clear signs of age. It was sent to the forensic laboratory of the University for examination.

Most parents were alarmed, fearing their own children might inadvertently be initiated into paganism during the night. Not a few turned to both the Police and the Church, requesting special policing measures.

Only indications and the reports of the Metropolitan. My personal opinion is that some children are simply having fun in an unusual way,' said a police officer from the Volos Police Directorate late in the evening.

The clergy of the area express their intense concern about what is taking place. They ask students to be careful and address the 'wayward' emphasizing that if they repent, the Church is ready to welcome them. 'They may have fallen into great errors. articles.title: Black Magic Ritual in Chalcis - 1994
articles.excerpt: Satanic symbols, nails and mysterious prayers were found at the Chalcis Lighthouse, left by a mysterious woman. The Church intervened and the finds were exorcised and burned.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1994 Evvoiki Gnomi newspaper article

content.value: The nightmare of black magic hangs over Chalcis, since according to the indications there continue to be individuals who occupy themselves with mysterious rituals, spells and prayers to Satan.

Satanic symbols, nails and mysterious prayers were found in the Lighthouse district, where a mysterious woman abandoned them, and the inhabitants of the area were thrown into agitation, following the recent events that shook the whole of Greece. “Gnomi” dealt with the black magic case on Tuesday, after an anonymous telephone call from a reader.
The Satanic symbols were found inside a bag, were exorcised by a priest and were then burned, following action by our newspaper and by the Holy Metropolis.
The chronicle of the affair is as follows:

At about ten in the morning a gentleman telephoned “Gnomi”, wishing to preserve his anonymity, and reported the following: together with a neighbour of his, a civil servant, he had seen a woman — tall, slim, dark-haired, in a red jacket — placing a nylon bag in the sea, on the shore that lies below the Lighthouse grove (in the Papathanasiou area). The dark-haired woman weighted the bag down beneath the water with a stone, a thing which aroused the curiosity of the two men.

A little later the bag began to float on the surface of the water. The two men went up to it, once the mysterious woman had gone, took the bag and found that it contained Satanic symbols. Specifically there was a wooden tablet with symbols of Satanism (pentagrams, dragons and so forth), numbers from 1 to 64, and nails.

There were also papers with unintelligible notes, a black stone and a text in an unintelligible dialect which resembled a prayer and which, according to the notes, had to be read 400 times. On the papers the name “Vosilis” was written.

The two gentlemen placed the bag with all the finds beside the locked gate at the entrance to the grove and telephoned the police at once. The Security Police, however, answered that they would intervene only upon a named complaint, while pointing out that the mere existence of the symbols does not constitute a criminal offence.

The next move of the “Gnomi” reader was to telephone the newspaper, which in its turn approached the Holy Metropolis. The Protosyngellos of the Metropolis, Fr Dionysios Mantolos, took an immediate interest and sent the parish priest of Agios Taxiarchis, under which the Lighthouse area falls, Archimandrite Ioannis Theodorakopoulos, to examine the finds.
And indeed, a short while later Fr Ioannis and two reporters of “Gnomi” were on the spot where the bag lay.

The newspaper’s staff at first treated the affair with scepticism, as was only natural. But Fr Ioannis, who has dealt with matters of black magic on behalf of the Church, gave it as his opinion that these were indeed Satanic symbols. Fr Ioannis read a prayer of exorcism at the place where the bag had been found, and then all the finds were consigned to the flames.

articles.title: Black Magic Rituals Volos - The Students of Satan - 1992
articles.excerpt: An open secret across all of Volos: black magic rituals by secondary school students, with a leader who 'kills with his gaze'. The Holy Metropolis of Dimitriados and preacher Fr. Daniel have been investigating the network for months.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1992 Eleftheros Typos newspaper article, pp. 32-33

content.value: — An open secret across the entire city: the black magic rituals and the leader who kills with his gaze.

'I came for you to read the prayer over my child, Father. He found a skull smeared with candles and plaster on the beach and came home terrified. His classmates do it, he says — works of Satan, diabolical things...'

The cry of anguish of the distressed mother fell like a thunderbolt on the Holy Metropolis of Dimitriados Volos, a little after Easter. It was the first report on the network of Satanist students that had for two years been infesting the schools of Volos, the thread for Metropolitan Christodoulos and Fr. Daniel to unravel...

Now Volos knows. Publications like yesterday's front page of 'E.T.' 'Black magic rituals by students of Volos' may have surprised all of Greece, but they were no bolt from the blue for the Thessalian city. The city's young people, for the most part, know about the students' acts of worship towards Satan — everyone has seen or heard something.

During break, in the schoolyard, at the café, the secondary school students of Volos openly discuss the 'rituals held at the full moon in the Goritsa grove', and describe the 'well-known' student-leader of the network, but give no names — only whispering, because 'those people' have 'that distant gaze that if you say something more, something bad might happen to you...'

How many of the 4,000 students of Volos's secondary schools are currently caught in Satan's net? 'Unknown,' admits preacher Danail Pourtsouкlis, appointed by Metropolitan Christodoulos to deal with matters of heresies and para-religion. 'The Metropolis's investigation has revealed that there are at least three different groups of student-propagandists of Satan-worship within the schools.
They gather children in abandoned houses in Volos or in the countryside and perform black magic rituals. Inspired by books and television, with the guidance perhaps of older people from Athens.'

The most 'popular' proselytizers: 'the triumvirate of final-year sixth-form students, with a female Satanist — a graduate herself.' Fr. Daniel knows the full name of the young man who 'goes out and tells children that Satanism will offer them success, and tries to impress his classmates and make them his subordinates through threats.' He knows that rituals with skulls and lit candles take place in Volos. No grave has been found desecrated.
Has anyone ever been endangered or injured in the rituals? The priest's refusal to answer breeds anxiety in the mind.

'I approached one of the leaders through a third party. I tried to inform his parents. They spoke of youthful nonsense and didn't care.' Then the threatening phone calls to the Holy Metropolis began. 'Altered voices telling me they would kill me, ordering me to stop the investigation...'

Technical, Polykladiko, 3rd, 5th, 1st Lyceum of Volos and secondary schools. The student world buzzes. The alphabet here gets mixed with Satan's symbols in the 'margins' of notebooks and the Solomonic mingles with school textbooks, as the children say.

'Did you come about the Satanism in the schools?' the theology teacher of the 3rd Lyceum, Papa-Ioannis Pappas, will ask. 'Quite a few children have gotten involved in Satanism. In Goritsa there is a grove where students gather when there is a full moon and perform mysterious rituals over circles and crescents drawn in the soil.' He too knows the 'leader' by name.
'I talk to them in class and there is also a relevant chapter in Religious Education.'

The students talk about Satanism in their schools as if discussing football, assuring they themselves stay away out of fear. 'If you join the network and perform a ritual, you've moved far from Christ. And if you say something about what you saw, something bad can happen to you. But curiosity pushes many people towards the rituals.'
No one speaks openly, 'better not to get labelled.'

About seven cats hung on the same branch in the park, a student will say, and another: 'There are candles, knives, words, keys of Satan and symbols carved in the desks.' A classmate describes triangular burns that 'some girls have on their wrist.'
“He is notorious,” they all say of the “leader” of the diabolical network.

They describe him as a “closed” character, “but open with his own people”. “He lives in Volos, he is in the sixth form, he has the Solomonic,” they know him by name, he might even be standing next to me, but the children will not give away the “leader” of the evil. “It is his eyes too, that look at you strangely, piercingly. Whatever you hear about him, believe it…”

articles.title: Church Burning by Satanists - Orchomenos 1995
articles.excerpt: On Christmas Day Satanists burned the church of Panagia Skripo in Orchomenos Boeotia, the second church destroyed in the area within 8 months. Meanwhile a couple was found dead in Sitia Crete with black magic symbols.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1995 Adesmeutos Typos newspaper article, pp. 24 & 41

content.value: Monday noon. Christmas Day. Dark moments for Christendom on the day of its greatest feast: at the very hour when Christians bow reverently before the miracle of the Nativity, others make a burnt offering of a church and rouse public opinion.
Rituals of black magic, enough to send a shiver through the coolest onlooker, unfolded at Orchomenos in Boeotia, branding its small society for the second time within eight months.

The church of Panagia Skripou of Orchomenos is reduced to ashes. The sculptures, the frescoes, the icons and the whole narthex are destroyed by the audacity and impiety of those who celebrate Satan on the day of Christ’s birth.

His small community is shaken. It grits its teeth and waits for the hour when the perpetrators of this abominable crime will be uncovered. The parish priest, Father Charalampos Hatzicharalampous, describes the incident, and his eyes fill with tears.
The firebomb

“As soon as the liturgy for Christmas Day had finished, we went home to eat. I lay down for a while. I was not feeling well. Suddenly I heard a child calling to me… ‘The church is burning, Father. The church is burning.’ I got up at once and went to see. The church had been engulfed in flames,” Father Charalampos tells us, and his voice breaks.

“This is the second time such a thing has happened. At Easter I had preached to the young people about Satanism, in a church a little further up, at the Holy Unmercenaries. That same day the telephone rang at the house and they told me: What you have done, you will regret.”

“Two days later the Holy Unmercenaries was given over to the flames. The church was completely destroyed. Exactly as the church of the Panagia was on 25 December. One pane of glass is broken; that is where they set the fire.”

The inhabitants of Orchomenos are in uproar. They threaten that if they find the perpetrators they will kill them with their own hands. Mrs Vassiliki Soulou tells “A.T.”: “They have destroyed us for the second time. If we had seen them we would have laid them out,” and she goes on: “This church was respected by Turks, by Bulgarians and by Germans, but it was not respected by Greeks. Here the greatest miracle took place, when the Panagia herself stopped the German tanks. The German commander of that battalion came here to venerate her until the day he died. And now the godless have burned her.”

And Giorgos Tatsis, a young man from Orchomenos, is categorical: “What has happened is a crime. The Fire Service told us it is out of the question that it was caused by a candle or by the oil lamps. A human hand did this. It is unbelievable.”

The church was built about 1,120 years ago, from the materials of an Early Christian temple. Today, despite the fire, it has not lost its splendour. Two young people were married there that afternoon, against the backdrop the flames had left behind. “I telephoned them to tell them the church had burned and the wedding could not take place,” says Father Charalampos. “They told me they did not care, that they had vowed to be married there. The whole village came to help with the cleaning up.”

The damage, according to the experts, is not only incalculable but irreparable. Father Charalampos, a tragic figure, sheds tears whenever he shows us the “beacon of the world”, as he characteristically calls it — the miracle-working icon of the Panagia.
It escaped the destruction and stands proud at the far end of the church.
A new cycle of blood begins.

At the very hour when Christ was being born, Satanists were revelling in rituals of black magic. An insult against the greatest feast of Christianity, in the most vulgar manner. They burned a church at Orchomenos to the glory of the “god of darkness” and committed sacrileges upon the things of God.

At the same time, a couple was found dead at Sitia in Crete, one of the two bodies beheaded. In the car of the two young people — murdered, or possibly sacrificed on the altar of Satan — symbols and objects of black magic ritual were found. Furthermore, on the man’s body a pendant was found with 666 engraved upon it, the symbol of the Antichrist.
Church bodies, and former members of Satanist organisations too, speaking to “A.T.”, express fear and anxiety that we stand before fresh crimes.
They maintain that the Satanists now act earlier than the appointed dates for rituals of black magic, so as to be difficult for the police authorities and the neighbours to detect.

The matter may take on still more tragic dimensions if one considers that we are shortly before January, in which, according to the Satanists’ calendar, two great Satanic festivals fall. On those days human sacrifices with the mutilation of limbs are provided for, as well as sexual orgies.
Commenting on these nightmarish phenomena, the press spokesman of the Holy Synod, Mr Hatzifotis, points to the atrocities committed by Dimitrokallis and his circle, at Christmas too, two years ago.

“I fear,” he told us, “that in combination with the recent incident in Crete we shall find ourselves once again before similar hideous situations. I believe that for the coming days policing should be intensified in the suspect districts where Satanist organisations have been active in the past.”

“This is a new tactic of the Satanists. They do not follow the appointed Satanic dates, and they act like lightning and outside their Satanic temples,” alleges Thanasis V., who was a leading member of the Satanists in Crete, and he continues: “In this way they believe they will not be noticed. They steal bones, they desecrate cemeteries, and they do not even hesitate to kill in order to carry out the ‘black rituals’ afterwards.”
The former Satanist, who wishes to keep his anonymity for obvious reasons, expresses the fear that a gang of Satanists exists in Crete which is operating systematically.

Cases such as the little girl who wrote the letter to Satan and afterwards took her own life, the abductions of girls, and the mass of reports of Satanic finds in hidden caves, prove the truth of what he says. All these facts are known to the Crete Police.
Fotis Nakos

articles.title: A Hodjas Sorcerer in Piraeus - 1893
articles.excerpt: A hodjas in Piraeus was deceiving women with promises of love potions, extracting over 500 drachmas from an unfortunate schoolteacher, until the police intervened following a complaint of fraud.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1893 To Asty newspaper article

content.value: Until now most sorcerers have been old women and itinerant Gypsies, with sorceries known and unknown, exploiting the simplest people — those who have not sufficient reason to be content with their lot. Now, however, there appears in Piraeus a hodja as well, worthily laying claim to the title of sorcerer.

Some time ago a retired schoolmistress, and a most unfortunate one in the matter of love, by the name of Eleni, had fallen victim to a well-known witch, in the hope of holding on, by means of various philtres, to her lover, who had given her bitter proofs of his infidelity. The police had intervened at the time, and the interrogations proved that she had given a very great deal of money to the witch, without any change coming over her unfaithful lover.

This refusal of his to stop being unfaithful evidently did not please the schoolmistress, and she tried by the same means to change his feelings towards her when she learned that in Piraeus there was a hodja, pious and conscientious in whatever spells he performed. The schoolmistress and a friend of hers went down to Piraeus to find him.

The hodja received the two young women, tried to console them for their unhappy situation, and then began his magic, sending them off with the arrangement that they should return after a few days to collect the philtre which would bring about the desired amorous constancy in the schoolmistress’s lover. It goes without saying that the two women’s repeated visits continued without any improvement in the affair — apart from the improvement in the hodja’s finances.

And perhaps that improvement would have continued for many years more, since he had already extracted from them over 500 drachmas, an exorbitant sum for the unfortunate schoolmistress’s slender means, had the hodja not proceeded to make certain declarations and demands that were to open the deceived women’s eyes a little. He asked them to stay in his house for a week, offering them his own room as well, the purpose being to make it easier for them all together to summon by night the spirit responsible, so that it might cure the trouble — for otherwise, he said, he could not achieve it on his own.
Fortunately the affair stopped at the sorcerer’s request, leaving the sequel to the police, to whom the charlatanry and fraud of the hodja-sorcerer were reported.

articles.title: The Modern Witches - 1933
articles.excerpt: Satirical article on the witches of the era and their methods: from pin-studded soap and water from thirty waves to conversing with stars and the enchantment of the eyes.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1933 Ethnos newspaper article

content.value: The modern witches are not ordinary beings, nor is witchcraft an easy business. Appearance plays a crucial role. The witch, to inspire confidence, must be a little dark or at least have the colour of filth approaching the swarthy complexion of the Gypsy.

This is the image of the witch that lives in the popular imagination. But there are also modern witches with fair complexions who practice this profession as amateurs. Such a witch could be your pretty neighbour, ready to read your cards or reveal your secrets in the coffee cup.

Magic, as we said, is not easy work either. The commonest method of sorcery among today’s witches is the pin-studded soap. And the man who reported to the police the young lady who had cast a spell on him produced this Satanic contrivance:
A piece of soap, a piece of cloth and a few pins.

It is well known what power soap contains — which witches systematically avoid when it comes to washing themselves, yet consider indispensable for magic. Besides soap, mysterious power is also contained in water collected from thirty waves. For this one obviously needs great patience, first choosing the location with great care. Glyfada, for example, is unsuitable, as is every beach that hosts mixed bathing — considered worldly and slightly depraved places.
Furthermore, the collector of waves must know how to swim a little, in case the thirtieth wave sweeps them away.

Another method is conversing with the stars, which puts to shame all astronomers who cannot manage communication with the planet Mars. Witches, without telescopes or calculations, have been conversing for so long not only with Mars but with the entire starry sky.

The most fearsome spells, however, are not those I have mentioned, nor are the most dangerous witches those who know the language of the stars and the power of soap. There are witches who employ only their charms and the expression of their eyes. They are the ones the poet tells us of:
With one glance of yours, witch, / from your sweet eyes, / like glass I cracked, / and broke into eight pieces.
Whether it was eight or seven or three pieces does not matter. Suffice it that the man was shattered and the guilty party was those beautiful eyes.

The victim of such a witch is certainly also the victim of the soap and pins. He reported the young lady who cast the ineffectual silly spell on him, and said not a word about the young lady who had truly bewitched him with her beautiful eyes. That is why we assume that women have no reason to collect thirty waves when they want to drown someone. They drown him with a smile. Men are so foolish.
T. Mor

articles.title: The Witch Who Found Husbands for Servants - 1933
articles.excerpt: Maria-Katina Polymenakous was arrested for fraud, deceiving servant women with promises of love spells and finding husbands, extracting thousands of drachmas from her victims.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1933 Foni tou Laou newspaper article

content.value: Following complaints lodged with the General Security Department by the servants Krystallia Vassiliadou and Zoi Papadopoulou, Maria-Katina Polymenakou, aged forty, was arrested yesterday at noon on a charge of fraud.

The woman arrested, presenting herself as a witch, deceived the two young women and received sums of money from them so that she might, by magic, procure them husbands. For the finding of her victims the witch made use of the servant Katina Roussou.
The latter, employed on Deligianni Street at the Olympos hotel, promised the victim that she would take her to an exceptional witch to cure her heartaches.

The naive Vassiliadou, persuaded by her friend’s words, went to 88 Agisilaou Street, to Polymenakou’s house, and recounted her love affair, in which she foresaw an inglorious end. She revealed to her that she loves a young man who of late has been trying to manufacture pretexts for abandoning her.
The spell did not take

The witch undertook to soften the friend’s hard heart. For this, however, much labour and expense would be required. The young woman gave the witch an advance of 300 drachmas, and in return she was given a small dagger which would act magically upon the young woman’s friend when it was placed beneath his pillow.

The night passed. The next day Krystallia, her hopes revived, found him as cold as on all the other occasions. Then followed another visit to the witch’s den. The magic dagger was described as a temporary spell. The witch would have to study an egg, which the young woman was to cut with the dagger. This would signify dominion over her chosen one. She would have him in her power from then on.

The notorious egg, however, was studied by the witch, who remained stark naked and covered with a white sheet on the roof terrace of her house. By her incantations she would achieve, so she told her victim, the disappearance of the white egg and the entry into it of the shadow of the victim’s friend. All this in the presence of witnesses. In this way the heavenly stars would be enlisted too.

The unfortunate young woman, obeying the witch’s promptings, agreed to make one more sacrifice, giving the witch another 2,850 drachmas for the conquest of her friend. The famous egg was studied. The young woman cut it with the magic dagger, but her friend’s heart remained unaltered. Then the young woman, disappointed by Polymenakou’s spells, made her way to the General Security and reported the fraud committed against her.

During the study of the magic egg, the witch’s accomplice, Maria Roussou, had found yet another victim: Zoi Papadopoulou, who was a servant at 2 Maizonos Street, in the house of the physician Mr Diamantis. This young woman, who had been working as a servant for years and saving her wages, had put together a dowry of 35,000 drachmas. She had been looking for a husband for a long time, but none appeared. Roussou promised her that she would introduce her to a fine young man, with whom she would attain an enviable happiness for the rest of her life.

This young man was Nik. Kontopoulos, whom she met through Roussou’s mediation. Kontopoulos, an agreeable and courteous young man, at once won the heart of his future wife. The witch’s accomplice advised her new victim as well to go to Polymenakou and ask her assistance towards the speedier fulfilment of her desires. And so it was done.

The next day the witch’s den played host to Papadopoulou. Once again an egg was studied beneath the stars and cut with a magic dagger. From these spells the naive young woman expected that the prospective bridegroom would very soon ask for her hand. Nor were her expectations disappointed. Kontopoulos presented himself to the physician Mr Diamantis and asked for the hand of his servant. Before the consent sought was given, information was gathered about the state of the prospective bridegroom. It was established, by an uncle of his, that he was a swindler.

The match was called off. The affair ended up at the General Security Department, where the relevant complaint was lodged. In it, it is stated that the witch received 3,000 drachmas from her victim for her services.

Sub-inspector Mr Sarantopoulos undertook to put a stop to the witch’s so profitable work. He went yesterday in plain clothes, accompanied by a young girl, to Agisilaou Street, to the witch’s den, where they met. The young woman played the part of his fiancée.
— I want you to tell me whether my fiancée loves me, he said to the witch.
— The coffee will tell you that.
And tell it did, in return for a fifty-drachma piece, which the officer duly paid.

Yesterday Mr Sarantopoulos visited the witch afresh. This time, however, not for her famous divination. He arrested her and took her to the police station, and she was tried in the flagrante court for sorcery and charlatanry.

In the witch’s den there was a small table with the magic eye painted upon it and various magical implements. A note was also found with 150 names written on it. The woman arrested will be sent within the day to the public prosecutor to be referred to an examining magistrate on the charge of fraud. So far no further victims of hers have come forward, but it is supposed that they are very many, given the nature of the profession.
In the flagrante magistrates’ court the witch Maria Polymenakou was sentenced to nine days’ detention on the charge of sorcery and charlatanry.

articles.title: A Thousand Sorcerers and Witches in Athens and Piraeus - 1933
articles.excerpt: Report on the methods of Athens's sorcerers, from the initial diagnosis-trap of victims to the rituals of the Pythia of Kimonos Street who caressed the moon naked on the roof tiles. Even a police officer was nearly convinced.

image.alt: Archival image from the 1933 Acropolis newspaper article

content.value: What lures the endless clientele into the clutches of the sorcerers is the initial diagnosis of the victim’s identity at the very first visit. It is like the old snare that holds the foolish birds captive with the barest few crumbs of bait.

Before any discussion at all, the sorcerer or the witch specifies to the victim the composition of his family, his name, the profession of the person he loves and other details. The naive victim is left dumbfounded. How does the sorcerer or the witch know so many things about him without his having told them anything?

Therefore he has superhuman qualities; therefore the sorcerer is capable of doing whatever is asked of him. The police officer Mr Mavrotas was very nearly convinced himself when he arrested the Dimitriadis with whom we are concerned. First of all the man told him that he was not a commercial employee, as Mr Mavrotas had claimed.
— You are a military man, he cried, stressing the syllables magnificently, as was his habit.
— No, no, we are in trade.
— No, said the sorcerer again. Crowns are falling beside you. If you are not bringing in crowns now, you will be bringing them in later.
Mr Mavrotas tried to conceal, as best he could, his agitation at the half-truth Dimitriadis had hit upon. His astonishment grew greater still when the sorcerer drew him aside and said to him:
— My dear boy, you are a young man. Do you love this woman very much?
— But of course. That is why I shall marry her.

It should be noted that Mr Mavrotas had presented a woman of loose morals as an acquaintance of his. The sorcerer therefore discerned that she was not an honest woman, and told him plainly — but into his ear, so that she should not hear:
— I see that she has many men about her, and you will be making a mistake if you take her.
Great tricks

All this shook the police officer. It was evident that the man possessed a power which not all men possess. But this power appears to have something otherworldly about it only to those who are ignorant of the reality. It is, as Mr Tanagras explains to us, ordinary intuition and telepathy. Countless people have it, and those who cultivate it through self-concentration have it the more. This fact is unknown to the inexhaustible clientele of the sorcerers, and it is with this that they are ensnared in the first place, so that afterwards they believe the sorcerers will hand them the sky with all its stars.
That was why Mr Mavrotas too was shaken; but his duty was to arrest the man, and he did so.
— Get dressed, he told him now, we are going to the police station. You made a mistake: I am a police officer.
And he moved towards him. Now Dimitriadis, with magnificent gestures and a suggestiveness that rooted the officer motionless where he stood, cried out:
— Do not move! Do not! You will lose your voice! Do not touch me!
The way in which he shouted, Mr Mavrotas tells us, was such that he was completely thrown.
Then the sorcerer, seeing that the trick had worked, raised his hands high and began to shout louder still:
— Lord! Lord Fanos! Burn him!
And he rang the bell like one possessed, so that the Lord — that is to say, Satan — should come.

But that dishonourable personage did not appear, Mr Mavrotas’s hands were not cut off, and the sorcerer was taken off to the station. Mr Mavrotas’s hands did come to some harm, however. A woman from the sorcerer’s staff — one who had once gone to ask his help over the heart of another man, and had ended up his mistress and his blind instrument — set upon the officer and bit his right hand. She too was taken to the police station, where she went on protesting at the arrest of a man of such power, who had done good to all the world and his brother.

Enormous faith in her initial diagnoses had likewise been won by the Pythia of Kimonos Street, Provata, with whom we dealt yesterday. She undertook not only to bring the faithless back into the warm embraces of the lovelorn, but also the cure of every disease. For example, she picked clean the property of a poor woman whose child had “the hour”.
— What do you mean, the hour? we asked her, and she muttered fearful curses against the sergeant Mr Panagiotopoulos, who had arrested her.

She sweated and sweated before she could explain it. This is the explanation of the explanation as given by the police: the young man who had “the hour” was seized by convulsions on account of a health problem in his respiratory organs. With the passage of time and his coming of age he would get well. But his mother could not bear to see him turning blue and often on the floor.

The Pythia undertook to consult the moon and her own judgement. For her judgement to work, hundreds of drachmas had to be paid. And in order to consult the moon she had to strip naked. Expenses, that is to say, of transport and of spectacle. And so, on the nights when the moon was waning, she would climb towards daybreak onto the roof terrace of the house, and from the terrace onto the tiles, where she then played Salome.

She would throw off her clothes and caress the moon with a veil. That, at least, was how she explained to her women clients the fact that she moved the veil naked towards the most peaceable Moon, and then moved it again, caressing her own aged body. articles.title: The Notorious Witch of Ilioupoli Arrested in Her Lair - 1955
articles.excerpt: The arrest of Anastasia Lamberaki, aged 45, a witch from Ilioupoli (Athens) who deceived wealthy women by invoking the spirit of Balaam through a glass crystal ball. A detailed account of her mystic den, her methods, and her psychological manipulation.

content.value: Officers of the Ilioupoli gendarmerie arrested Anastasia Lamberaki, aged 45, charged with defrauding various persons through the practice of sorcery. As established by the preliminary investigation, she received various women of the upper class at her home in the Ymittos district, telling their fortunes and providing advice on matters of the heart in exchange for payment of many thousands of drachmas.

To lend greater mystery to her sessions with clients, the witch had transformed her home into an evocative lair: the four walls were draped in black fabric, the lighting was low and concealed, and various magical objects were arranged on a table, where pride of place was given to a glass crystal ball.

The client was led into this room and seated facing the table, with the witch sitting behind her. This first impression, as was natural, acted powerfully on the women's psychology; the shift from bright light to the half-darkness of the suggestive room inspired awe and rendered the clients receptive from the outset to the witch's pronouncements.

In this psychological state, the client would unburden herself, and the witch would undertake to assist through her art in resolving the problems at hand. To this end, she began to pray and to invoke the spirit of Balaam, a renowned pagan soothsayer mentioned in the Bible. Before completing the prayer, and without being noticed, the witch would use a hidden electric switch to cut the concealed lighting and illuminate a mysterious light focused on the crystal ball.

Within the sphere, due to the nature of the glass, various mysterious light-and-shadow effects were produced, which the entranced client interpreted as supernatural visions arising from the appearance of the spirit of Balaam. The witch then proceeded to question the spirit about whatever concerned her victim, and — according to the shadows produced — she interpreted corresponding answers, which she recorded in kabbalistic symbols while simultaneously whispering various unintelligible words. When there were no further questions of interest to the victim, the witch extinguished the sphere's light by the same secret mechanism and re-lit the room's general concealed lighting.

One of the victims, a well-known lady whose name is not given, sought the witch's help in winning back the love of her husband, who had been neglecting her while conducting a parallel affair with a dancer. The spirit of Balaam, according to the witch, recommended the following to detach the unfaithful husband from the dancer's embrace:

You will take nine hairs from your own hair and as many from your husband's, and having braided them on a night of the full moon, three by three, you will wrap them in this paper. You will place this paper with the six braids under your pillow. After three days and three nights, you will take it in the evening before the next full moon and re-braid the six braids three by three again under the moonlight. The two braids that result you will place again in this paper, and this time you will put them inside your husband's pillow, between the pillowcase and the pillow, so he notices nothing. There you will leave them until the full moon. The man must sleep on that pillow on the night of the full moon, otherwise the spell will be broken. Once he has slept there, the next day you will take it; one braid you will burn together with the paper as soon as the moon rises, and scatter the ash outside your house. The other you will place in your husband's jacket, inside the lining where he cannot find it, and all will be well.

The victim, who had paid 1,000 drachmas for the famous recipe, returned three months later to complain, as her husband continued his relationship with the dancer. The witch, accustomed to such complaints, had a ready answer:

"My dear, you must have done something wrong! Had you done exactly as I told you, you would have won your husband back."
"Shall I do it all over from the beginning? Would you be so kind as to write the recipe out again so I can be careful to do it properly this time?"
"Oh, my dear! And do you think I remember what I told you? Do you think I can repeat it without making mistakes myself? I was writing down whatever the spirit told me. I gave you the paper. You burned it. What can I tell you now? We must summon the spirit once more. And will the great Balaam appear again? What you are doing is irreverence — the spirits grow angry. I will do what I can for you, but it is difficult."

These words proved sufficiently persuasive, as the victim agreed to attend a new summoning of the spirit of Balaam — who, however, required the witch to suffer greatly before agreeing to appear and provide a new recipe. This reluctance on the spirit's part was performed before the credulous lady at a cost of 1,500 drachmas.

The witch did not always employ the same method. Especially during the summer months, when the atmosphere of the evocative room was stifling, she would lead her clients outdoors, to the Mamais estate in the Ilioupoli district. There, between 9 and 12 at night, among the trees and under the starry sky, she would invoke the spirits — sometimes Balaam, sometimes Lucifer, sometimes other demons — having first compelled her victim to cover their eyes with a piece of their own undergarment, instructing them not to turn their head left, right, or backward, as the spirit would not appear in that case.

The witch, standing behind the victim, then began to invoke the spirit with unintelligible words, among which only the name of the summoned spirit could be distinguished. To the questions she put to the spirit, she herself answered in a muffled voice, feigning a dialogue. When finished, she would take from her bag a recipe prepared in advance and tell the victim to remove the undergarment from their eyes. She would then hand over the recipe with instructions for its execution. Through this method, the arrested witch amassed considerable sums, as her clientele was enormous.

After her interrogation by the commander of the Ilioupoli gendarmerie station, she claimed that she did not invoke evil spirits but the help of God. And when she mentioned Lucifer in her invocations, she was not seeking his help but rather his defeat by the Divine powers. The witch was transferred after her interrogation to the Public Prosecutor.

articles.excerpt: A 1895 newspaper piece about a priest who, unable to be cured by earthly or heavenly doctors, turned to a witch from Argos and was miraculously restored to health, and about a lady from Tripoli who also sought the help of sorcery.

content.value: Such a decline in Christian values has lately been observed that many seek their healing and their fortune through magic.

A priest, who had failed to recover through the doctors of earth and heaven, turned to a witch from Argos whom he summoned with such certainty that, after her visit, he became — miraculously — fully restored to health, as he himself swears.
And another lady from Tripoli, whose name we shall not mention for the present, sought the assistance of sorcery. She herself attests to being cured of a long-standing illness.

Unfortunately, we do not possess the scientific authority to establish how far we are regressing, or which ancient age of darkness and ignorance our present state may be compared to. For this reason, we turn to our bishop, Mr. Vimpos, who, being well versed in Hebrew, is perfectly capable of enlightening us on the above matter.

articles.title: Igoumenitsa: Doll with Nails in Its Eyes Found on a Beach
articles.excerpt: A doll with nails driven into its head, bound cloth and vivid red markings was found on the beach of Drepano, Igoumenitsa, sparking alarm and associations with black magic rituals.

image.alt: Doll with nails and red markings found on the beach of Drepano, Igoumenitsa

content.value: A macabre find caused alarm on the beach of Drepano in Igoumenitsa. A doll, discarded in the sand, was found with nails driven into its head, bound pieces of cloth and vivid red colouring on its face and neck, causing considerable distress to those who came across it.

The image of the doll, placed among driftwood washed up on the shore, evoked a scene of dark symbolism. Many linked the find to black magic rituals or other occult practices, in keeping with the popular imagination that surrounds such objects.

Despite the speculation, neither the origin of the object nor any actual connection to a ritual can be confirmed. Nevertheless, the elements of the scene — the nails, the red colouring resembling blood, and the overall staging — reinforced the associations and caused unease among those present.

The incident carries particular weight given that the Drepano beach is one of the best-known and most frequented in the area. The presence of such an unsettling object in a public space provoked strong reactions and comment.

Drepano is a landmark destination for Igoumenitsa, especially during the summer months when visitor numbers increase. The sight of a doll with such features, left in plain view, understandably caused a stir.
Many people connected the find with 'curse rituals', voodoo practices or other forms of symbolic energy, familiar from folk horror stories and occultism.
This article is a republication from the Ta Nea newspaper.
